title: Sound
content: Sound is a sequence of pressure wave which propagates through compressible media such as air or water.
e: Sound is a pressure wave that needs a compressible medium such as air or water. Molecules push on their neighbours and the disturbance travels. Vacuum has nothing to compress, so sound cannot cross it.

title: Speed of sound wave
content: Speed of sound wave can also be affected by the density, temperature and elasticity of the medium through which the sound waves travel.
e: The speed of sound is set by how density and pressure in the medium respond, and temperature changes that link. Elasticity also matters. Frequency and amplitude do not set the travel speed in a given medium.

title: Intensity Level of Sound
content: The level of intensity of a sound is measured relative to a reference intensity value taken as 10^-12 W m^-2 which correspond to the minimum intensity of sound that can be heard (threshold of hearing or minimum audible intensity).
e: Intensity level compares a sound to a reference intensity of 10^-12 W m^-2, the threshold of hearing. That reference is the quietest sound a normal ear can detect. Pain threshold and ultrasound are different numbers.

title: Decibel (dB)
content: The decibel (dB) is the unit used for measuring sound intensity (intensity level of sound).
e: The decibel is the unit of sound intensity level, a logarithmic comparison with the hearing threshold. Hertz measures frequency and watt measures power. Loudness roughly jumps tenfold for every extra 10 dB.

title: Echo
content: Echos are produced when a sound wave is reflected from a large and hard surface. An echo is repetition of sound due to the reflection of sound.
e: An echo is a repeat of a sound after reflection from a large hard surface. Soft padding swallows the wave instead of sending it back. Distance follows from the go-and-return time if you know the speed.

title: Audibility
content: Audible means able to be heard. Audibility means the ability to be heard or capability of detecting sounds in certain range of frequencies.
e: Audibility is the ability to detect sound in a band of frequencies. It is not just loudness and not just amplitude. Humans with normal hearing sit roughly between 20 Hz and 20 000 Hz.

title: Range of audibility
content: The range of frequencies a person can hear is known as the range of audibility.
e: The range of audibility is the frequency interval a person can hear. Typical human limits are about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Sounds outside that window can still exist; the ear just does not register them as tone.

title: Limit of audibility
content: For humans with normal hearing, the lower limit is 20Hz and the upper limit is about 20000 Hz. These limits are known as limit of audibility.
e: The limits of audibility are those lower and upper frequencies, about 20 Hz and 20 000 Hz for normal human hearing. Below 20 Hz you may feel vibration without hearing a note. Above 20 000 Hz the sound is ultrasound.

title: Infrasound
content: Low frequency sounds which are under the lower limit of audibility (20 Hz) are called infrasound and cannot be heard by human.
e: Infrasound is sound below 20 Hz, under the lower hearing limit. Humans do not hear it as a tone. Long infrasonic waves can travel far, which is a different tool from medical ultrasound.

title: Ultrasound
content: High frequency sounds which are above the upper limit of audibility (20000 Hz) are called ultrasound which cannot be heard by human ear.
e: Ultrasound is sound above about 20 000 Hz, beyond the upper hearing limit. The human ear misses it, but the short wavelength is useful for imaging, cleaning, and echolocation. Sonar and medical scanners lean on those echoes.

title: Sonar
content: The sonar (sound navigation and ranging) is type of technology that works based on echoes.
e: Sonar, sound navigation and ranging, times echoes to find range and direction underwater. It is echolocation with a loudspeaker and a microphone. Radar does a similar job with radio waves, not sound.

title: Doppler effect
content: The Doppler effect or Doppler shift is the change in frequency of wave related to an observer due to the relative motion between the source and the observer.
e: The Doppler effect is the change in observed frequency when source and observer move relative to each other. Approach packs the waves and raises the pitch. Recession stretches them and lowers the pitch.

title: Red shift
content: The wavelength the light from star observed from the earth's shift due to Doppler effect towards the red end of the spectrum (lower frequency, longer wavelength) when the earth and the star are moving away from each other. This phenomenon is called red shift.
e: Red shift is a Doppler slide of light toward longer wavelength and lower frequency. It appears when the source and the observer move apart. A blue shift is the opposite motion, toward each other.

title: Rader
content: Rader (radio detection and ranging) is a form of echolocation that uses electromagnetic waves instead of sound but otherwise the concept is similar.
e: Radar, radio detection and ranging, is echolocation that uses electromagnetic waves instead of sound. The timing idea is the same as sonar. Bats, by contrast, hunt with sound echoes.

title: Pitch
content: The pitch of the note (how high it is) is determined by its frequency. The greater the frequency, the higher is the pitch.
e: Pitch is how high a note sounds, and frequency is what sets it. Raise the frequency and the pitch rises. Amplitude changes loudness, not the high-or-low character of the note.

title: Quality or Timbre
content: Timbre is the quality of the sound which allows us to distinguish between different sound producing sound at the same pitch and loudness.
e: Timbre, or quality, lets you tell a violin from a flute when pitch and loudness match. The waveform and its overtones carry that colour. Extra harmonics make a richer note.
